quests.scene: Ferrum's operators keep old search results open while editing the source archive. The original parser returns borrowed fields from a buffer that the editor wants to replace. One quick fix copies every field; another stores references inside the object that owns the editable string. Your endgame begins by deciding what an old result means after an edit. Storage, identity, and the version of the text must tell the same story.
quests.objective: Design parsed document snapshots whose records remain meaningful while a newer document version is edited.
win_conditions: Keep each retained record tied to the exact source version from which its ranges were produced.
Preserve UTF-8 range validity without storing movable internal self references.
Explain the memory cost of retaining a tiny result from a large old document.
quests.boss_brief: Extend the borrowing-parser design into an editor model with immutable source snapshots. A reader can retain a record from version A while the editor produces version B. Design owners and byte ranges so the old record still resolves to A and cannot silently index B. An API accepting a free-standing span must reject use with an unrelated snapshot or make that mismatch impossible through ownership. Define how invalid text produces owned diagnostics without exposing an invalid record. Show the lifetime and retention consequences of returning a temporary borrowed view versus an independently owned record handle. Your deliverable should include a complete ownership diagram and tests for edits that change byte lengths before a retained field.
constraints: Do not mutate a source allocation while retained views rely on its old contents.
Avoid a structure storing ordinary references into its own movable owned String.
Do not confuse Unicode character positions with byte offsets.
quests.debrief: An immutable snapshot can own one source string and its validated ranges. A temporary view borrows that snapshot; an independently retained record can carry an ownership share of the exact snapshot plus a record index. Moving handles leaves ranges meaningful because resolution uses their associated owner. If spans travel independently, attach and validate a snapshot identity rather than assuming equal numeric offsets imply equal text. Editing constructs a new snapshot instead of mutating A beneath its readers. Owned diagnostic positions survive rejection without granting a valid record. Sharing avoids copying every field but retains the complete old source, so selective copying may still be the best policy for a few long-lived search results.
quests.hint1: Give the old text and the new text different names. Then follow one retained field after an insertion at the beginning. Which owner or identity prevents its old byte range from resolving against the new bytes?
quests.hint2: Separate immutable source snapshots from the editor's current-snapshot handle. Store validated ranges, not internal references, and construct borrowed views on demand. A retained record can own a shared snapshot handle and an index. Check every boundary before slicing, and make source identity part of span resolution when the span does not already own its source.
quests.side_quest: Add normalized search keys while preserving exact original spelling for display. For ASCII-only case normalization, decide whether keys borrow or own bytes and where they are cached. Then discuss what changes when normalization can change byte length. Keep normalized offsets separate from source spans, and measure the cost of caching keys for records that are never searched. Keep display text independent from lookup policy.

route_choices.label: Make history transactional
route_choices.reason: Add an explicit validation rule when snapshots become the basis of writes.

route_choices.label: Revisit lending views
route_choices.reason: Compare reusable producer storage with independently retained document records.

quests.reward: Snapshot Pathfinder

quests.scene: The restored archive lets an operator preview a repair, try a risky adjustment, and discard only that adjustment. Ferrum calls these inner experiments savepoints. The existing store knows how to validate one transaction against its snapshot, but the operator now needs nested local work that does not leak into the published map. Your challenge is to distinguish committing a child proposal from publishing a new global version.
quests.objective: Add nested local savepoints while preserving the outer transaction’s snapshot and global commit validation.
win_conditions: Child rollback leaves parent staged reads and writes unchanged.
Child commit merges only into the parent proposal and never independently publishes store state.
A conflicting outer commit rejects the complete nested proposal without partially publishing it.
quests.boss_brief: Design savepoints for the versioned store. A parent transaction stages a value, a child reads it and changes two keys, and the child can either merge or roll back. Reads should consult the nearest staged change before older layers and the base snapshot. A child deletion must hide an older value rather than look like no staged entry. Only the outer transaction may call the store’s publication operation. Provide histories covering child rollback, child merge followed by parent rollback, and a background writer invalidating the outer base before publication. Explain what remains a valid historical snapshot after conflict. You may use an owned transaction stack or a scoped borrowing API, but identify who owns every staged value at each transition.
constraints: Do not advertise independent database isolation for these local savepoints.
Preserve store-origin validation as well as version validation.
No external side effects occur merely because an inner savepoint merges.
quests.debrief: A savepoint layer is a proposal overlay, not a new published store. Reads search from the newest layer outward, distinguishing a tombstone from absence in that layer. Rollback discards the child’s owned changes. Merge moves those changes into its parent while leaving the same base snapshot and outer validation requirements intact. Only a successful outer publication advances the store version and replaces visible state. If a background writer invalidates the base, rejecting the outer transaction discards the whole combined proposal; its historical snapshot remains valid for reading. Retain the identity check that prevents a transaction from another store passing on an equal numeric version. Nested structure does not make external effects reversible.
quests.hint1: Rename child commit to merge while designing it. That word makes the missing distinction visible: one action changes a local proposal, while another publishes a new store state for all readers.
quests.hint2: Use a stack of maps whose values distinguish replacement from deletion. A lookup checks the newest map first and stops at the first staged entry, including a tombstone. Merging moves entries into the immediately older map. The base snapshot and origin identity remain attached to the outer transaction until its final validation.
quests.side_quest: Allow a long-running preview to report which keys it changed without claiming those values are still current. Design a conflict report that separates reusable owned input from calculations derived from stale reads. Then compare retrying the whole decision with merging a domain-specific commutative operation. State the conditions that make the latter legitimate rather than treating every conflict as mergeable. Test a conflicting concurrent writer as well.

route_choices.label: Move proposals through workers
route_choices.reason: Preserve ownership and accounting while work crosses bounded queues.

route_choices.label: Review the consistency claim
route_choices.reason: Check precisely which state the version rule validates.

quests.reward: Savepoint Architect

quests.scene: Ferrum's workers are fast enough to overwhelm their collector. Bounded channels keep queues small until the collector fails, after which the coordinator waits for workers and the workers wait for result capacity. Every allocation still has a valid owner, yet the city stops. This boss tests the difference between safe memory and a live shutdown protocol. The escape route follows who can close each queue and who observes that closure.
quests.objective: Make collector failure terminate a bounded finite pipeline without detached workers or a cyclic wait.
win_conditions: Trace the wait graph when the result receiver disappears under backpressure.
Join every worker and classify undelivered versus previously accepted jobs honestly.
Reproduce collector failure with deterministic synchronization at small queue capacities.
quests.boss_brief: Adapt the worker pipeline so its collector can return an ordinary error after receiving a chosen result. The result queue and input queues are bounded. Arrange a test where dispatch is still active at that moment. Specify how closing the result receiver reaches workers, how workers stop accepting further work, and how a coordinator blocked in send eventually observes disconnection. Join every thread even after the first failure. Distinguish the message returned by a failed send from jobs that a worker previously accepted or started. For pure finite computations, define which abandoned jobs may be retried; for external effects, allow an uncertain classification. Your solution must not rely on a cancellation flag waking an unrelated blocking operation.
constraints: Assume each active computation eventually returns; do not promise interruption of arbitrary blocking I/O.
Every remaining sender and receiver owner has a documented shutdown role.
Error reporting must not introduce a second bounded queue that nobody drains.
quests.debrief: Dropping the collector’s receiver causes workers’ pending or later result sends to fail. Workers then exit their input loops and drop receivers, allowing a coordinator blocked on an affected input send to observe disconnection. This progress argument depends on active computations eventually reaching that send or another shutdown check. Drop coordinator input senders and retain panic payloads until all joins finish. A send error returns the specific undelivered message. Track earlier accepted jobs by ID and classify their outcomes separately. An atomic cancellation flag alone does not wake a blocked send or recv. Keep any final reporting path bounded by a justified amount or independently drainable.
quests.hint1: Draw arrows from each blocked operation to the component that can release it. Then remove the result receiver. Which workers wake immediately, which must first finish computation, and which owner keeps the coordinator’s send connected?
quests.hint2: Treat channel disconnection as part of the protocol. Result-send failure should lead to dropping the relevant job receiver, rather than waiting for more jobs forever. Join every handle explicitly after admission closes. Add a test hook that confirms dispatch is active before the collector fails, and use capacities zero or one to expose hidden waiting cycles.
quests.side_quest: Replace pure arithmetic with a simulated remote operation that can complete before its acknowledgment is lost. Record job IDs and attempts in the simulator. Show why replaying a previously accepted job may duplicate an effect even though replaying the payload of a failed input send does not. Add a domain-specific idempotency policy and test its required peer behavior separately. Keep the admission boundary explicit throughout.

route_choices.label: Negotiate uncertain outcomes
route_choices.reason: Represent what the peer may have done when local confirmation disappears.

route_choices.label: Return to service supervision
route_choices.reason: Generalize finite pipeline shutdown into a service lifecycle.

quests.reward: Shutdown Warden

quests.scene: Ferrum reopens a communication route, sends a repair command, and loses the connection before an acknowledgment arrives. One operator calls the command failed and retries with a new identifier. Another calls it successful because the bytes were written. Both know less than they claim. Your protocol map needs a place for uncertainty, and the permission to retry must depend on an explicit peer contract rather than optimism.
quests.objective: Represent reconnect and retry decisions without confusing local transport status with confirmed remote effects.
win_conditions: Model pending, confirmed, and unknown outcomes distinctly.
Preserve operation identity across a retry when the chosen protocol requires deduplication.
Test a peer that executes a command but drops its acknowledgment.
quests.boss_title: The Echo That May Already Exist
quests.boss_brief: Design a client-side command state machine for a fake peer. The peer may execute a command and then lose its reply. The client supports reconnect, querying status when the peer protocol permits it, and an explicit retry policy. Choose which transitions should consume typed capabilities and which belong in a runtime enum. A disconnect after sending must not automatically become a confirmed failure. Define the stable operation ID, the peer’s deduplication or status-retention contract, and what happens when that retention expires. Build a deterministic simulation of lost acknowledgment, duplicate delivery, and confirmed rejection before execution. Explain what your Rust types guarantee locally and what remains dependent on the peer’s behavior.
constraints: Do not claim exactly-once execution from ownership or a successful local write.
An unknown outcome cannot silently convert into safe retry authorization.
Scope the simulator explicitly; it is not a deployed distributed transaction system.
quests.debrief: A local state machine can prevent phase confusion and preserve the operation ID, but it cannot infer an unseen remote outcome. After an ambiguous disconnect, move to an unknown state. Querying status or retrying with the same ID is useful only under a peer contract that retains and recognizes the necessary history. Expiration may restore uncertainty rather than prove nonexecution. Confirmed rejection before execution is a different outcome and can permit a new attempt under the stated policy. Use typed capabilities when a transition genuinely removes an operation, and runtime alternatives when a manager must hold mixed states. The fake peer should independently record effects so tests can detect duplicate execution behind lost replies.
quests.hint1: List what the client observed and what the peer could have done. If two remote histories produce the same local observation, the client’s next state must accommodate both unless another protocol event distinguishes them.
quests.hint2: Give the command a stable logical ID separate from its connection and attempt number. Simulate execution followed by a dropped reply. Reconnection alone supplies no missing acknowledgment. An explicit unknown state forces callers to choose status lookup, deduplicated retry under a real contract, or manual recovery instead of treating every error as safely repeatable.
quests.side_quest: Add a process restart between command execution and acknowledgment handling. Decide where the client stores operation identity and recovery state, and what the peer must retain. A process-local HashMap is not durable history. Draw the crash windows around each persistence step and describe which outcomes remain uncertain when either side loses its remembered state. Treat forgotten recovery records as uncertainty, too.

route_choices.label: Ship the protocol as an API
route_choices.reason: Expose uncertainty and recovery without making accidental compatibility promises.

route_choices.label: Return to cancellation terrain
route_choices.reason: Connect dropped local computations to effects that may continue elsewhere.

quests.reward: Uncertainty Navigator

quests.scene: The city’s repaired components are ready to become a library used outside Ferrum. The release candidate passes its own tests, but an integration crate no longer spawns one returned future, a minimal build imports an unavailable module, and the package omits a schema file. This gate tests whether a release is the artifact downstream users actually compile. Public promises include configurations and properties that never appear in the happy-path demonstration.
quests.objective: Validate a release through representative downstream callers and the packaged artifact rather than only the development checkout.
win_conditions: Create downstream compile fixtures for the public ownership, error, and future bounds you intend to support.
Exercise minimal and relevant feature configurations instead of assuming all-features covers them.
Build the packaged artifact with its declared inputs and compiler support policy.
quests.boss_brief: Prepare a small library release with a protocol core and an optional adapter. Create two consumer fixtures: one uses the minimal configuration and one requires a returned future to be Send while borrowing suitable input. Now review a proposed change that adds Rc across a suspension point, narrows a generic bound, adds a variant to an exhaustive error enum, and references a workspace-only schema in a build script. Decide which changes violate your stated promises and which require an explicit compatibility decision. Validate the actual packaged source, not just local files. Your deliverable includes the support matrix, meaningful compile checks, the package contents you inspected, and release notes written around observable caller consequences.
constraints: Do not claim minimum compiler support without checking the declared baseline.
Keep optional features composable according to Cargo’s resolved feature behavior.
A local successful build is not evidence that omitted package inputs are available to users.
quests.debrief: Downstream fixtures test the interface properties callers rely on without naming anonymous future types. A helper requiring Send can detect the Rc regression; a borrowed-input fixture separately tests lifetime flexibility. Narrower bounds and exhaustive error changes need compatibility review rather than being dismissed as internal edits. Minimal configurations expose imports hidden by default or maximal builds. Package inspection and building from the package detect workspace-only assumptions. Declare generated inputs and distinguish host execution from target properties in build scripts. The compiler baseline is a separate tested dimension. Release notes should explain changed caller obligations and behavior, while avoiding claims of universal compatibility based only on one preferred configuration.
quests.hint1: Pretend the release archive is all the next developer receives. Which tests depend on files, features, or compiler properties that exist only in your working checkout? Write a consumer that states one promised bound directly.
quests.hint2: Use small compile fixtures rather than copying production implementations into tests. Require Send on the produced future through a generic helper, then separately exercise supported borrowed inputs. Test the minimal feature set and meaningful combinations, inspect packaged files, and build those files under the declared support conditions. Configuration coverage should follow concrete promises.
quests.side_quest: Design an upgrade guide for a deliberate breaking change to error recovery and compiler baseline. Include one short before-and-after caller example and a migration check. Then identify one implementation change that should remain invisible to consumers. Explain how documentation can accidentally turn an incidental layout, allocation count, or cancellation detail into a future compatibility commitment. Make each promised migration step verifiable.

route_choices.label: Face the final audit
route_choices.reason: Combine published promises with the invariants and evidence behind them.

route_choices.label: Reforge the API boundary
route_choices.reason: Reconsider which extensibility and compatibility choices belong in public types.

quests.reward: Compatibility Sentinel

quests.scene: Ferrum’s map is connected again, but restoring each district separately did not prove the whole city coherent. A borrowed parser can retain old storage. A bounded worker queue can hide an unbounded producer. A valid local state machine can still retry an uncertain remote effect. The final encounter brings these boundaries together. Your artifact is a small working simulation and an explanation a skeptical developer can inspect, challenge, and extend.
quests.objective: Build and defend one coherent in-memory system whose ownership, state, progress, and verification claims agree.
win_conditions: Trace one request from source ownership through validation, work admission, state change, and reported outcome.
Demonstrate a deterministic failure history and preserve the documented accounting or uncertainty state.
Separate type-enforced guarantees, runtime invariants, and assumptions about another component.
quests.boss_brief: Build a finite repair simulator using the book’s ideas: immutable parsed configuration, a versioned local store, bounded work admission, and a fake remote peer that can lose replies. Choose a modest scenario such as updating station settings. Implement enough of the path to run a successful request, a stale transaction, and a lost acknowledgment. Supply an ownership diagram, a wait graph, and three precise invariants. For each invariant, name the implementation mechanism and evidence that supports it. Introduce one controlled failure after acceptance and show the reported outcome without silently losing the request or claiming the remote effect never occurred. Unsafe code is optional; if used, include its proof obligations and explain why the safe representation was insufficient.
constraints: Keep the scope finite and runnable without a real network or deployed database.
Do not claim durability, exactly-once delivery, or proof of soundness from the simulator.
Any memory bound must name queues, payload retention, snapshots, and admitted work.
quests.debrief: A strong solution makes each boundary explicit rather than maximizing features. Parsed views resolve against their owning snapshot. Admission transfers a job identity and the resources needed to account for it. Store publication validates the right origin and version before committing prepared state. Worker and collector shutdown release the channel owners needed for progress. The fake peer records effects independently, so a lost reply produces an unknown outcome until the chosen protocol resolves it. Tests attack these claims with deliberate histories. Types prevent particular invalid accesses and transitions; runtime checks enforce lengths, versions, and budgets; peer assumptions govern remote semantics. The final argument should state those limits directly and connect every claimed guarantee to actual evidence.
quests.hint1: Choose one request and draw every owner it passes through. At each boundary ask what can fail, who still owns partial progress, and which observation authorizes the next transition. One unexplained arrow is a useful place to attack.
quests.hint2: Keep three columns in your review: enforced by types, checked at runtime, and assumed from a protocol. Put each invariant in the correct column, then name its test or argument. A bounded queue belongs only to part of a memory bound; a local Result belongs only to part of an outcome protocol. Use the fake peer’s independent effect log to expose that distinction.
quests.side_quest: Invite another developer to choose one hostile change: a retained old snapshot, a forgotten guard, a collector failure, a malformed frame, or a reused operation ID. Predict which invariant it challenges before running anything. Repair the design or narrow the promise, then update the evidence. Your final achievement is the ability to explain the repair, not merely to recover a passing test.

route_choices.reason: Revisit representation choices with the complete system’s ownership and measurement evidence.

rooms.title: The Vanishing Archive
rooms.brief: A log service parses a 256 MiB input buffer. Downstream work retains only a 24-byte identifier from each selected record for several minutes. The input must then be reused for the next batch. Your benchmark rewards low allocation counts, but the incident report complains about peak live memory. Choose a representation before you inspect the consequences. Assume the selected identifiers are a small fraction of the original buffer and do not need to preserve the original allocation identity.

choices.label: Keep slices into the reusable buffer
choices.result: The borrowing relationship prevents reuse while the slices remain usable. That compiler error identifies the incompatible storage policy. Extending annotations does not make the buffer independent. This choice works if consumers finish before reuse or if you change the owner and stop reusing this allocation; it does not meet the requirements as stated.

choices.label: Retain an Arc to the whole batch
choices.result: Shared ownership keeps the original bytes alive for views or validated ranges. It also prevents overwriting those bytes while readers still need them, and one tiny identifier retains the entire 256 MiB. This design fits a different contract that allows a separate receive buffer and makes dense retention worth its memory cost.

choices.label: Copy the selected identifiers at the queue boundary
choices.result: The queue owns compact strings independent of the batch. This deliberately spends allocations and byte copies to release the much larger source and permit reuse. Measure selected-byte volume and allocator costs, but compare them against peak retained memory rather than declaring zero-copy the winner by definition.

rooms.remix: Downstream analysis now retains nearly every byte. The producer may rotate to another receive buffer while readers retain the old one. Re-evaluate the three actions and explain how retention density and the number of live batches affect your choice.

rooms.title: The Ghost Payment
rooms.brief: A request future times out after sending a payment command. The connection then disappears. Your local request value is dropped cleanly. The remote service may have processed the command, but no acknowledgement reached you. The business requires that one purchase must not be charged twice. Choose your next action. The service has a status lookup and an idempotency-key mechanism, but their retention and deduplication contracts must be checked.

choices.label: Retry immediately with a fresh operation identifier
choices.result: A new identifier can make the retry look like a second purchase. Dropping the future did not reverse the remote effect. This action is suitable only if duplicate execution is acceptable or another layer prevents it; the stated purchase invariant does not permit that assumption.

choices.label: Reuse the key and treat deduplication as automatic
choices.result: A stable key is useful only under the peer's documented scope, retention period, payload matching, and failure behavior. If the record expires before retry or different payloads share a key, your local type cannot repair the protocol. First establish the remote contract rather than treating the presence of a key field as a guarantee.

choices.label: Record an uncertain outcome and reconcile under the peer contract
choices.result: Keep the original operation identity and the exact request meaning. Consult the peer's status and idempotency behavior, then retry or reconcile according to that contract. An inconclusive lookup may leave the outcome uncertain. This is an explicit protocol state, not a reason to manufacture a success or failure locally.

rooms.remix: Remove the status endpoint and give idempotency records a finite lifetime. Design an escalation path for an unresolved purchase approaching expiry. Identify what must become a human or business decision instead of an unbounded automatic retry.

rooms.title: The Hollow Lock
rooms.brief: A shared cache calls a slow user-supplied loader while holding its global mutex. The loader can recursively request another key, and two requests for the same key can trigger an expensive external operation. Product wants low contention and one active loader per key. Choose an initial redesign. A valid answer must account for reentrancy, failure, and abandoned loads rather than merely moving a lock statement.

choices.label: Keep the global lock and forbid nothing else
choices.result: The recursive call can attempt to acquire the mutex already held by the loader. A global lock also serializes unrelated keys. This does not satisfy the stated reentrancy and contention requirements. A non-reentrant contract could be a different design, but it must be explicit and still needs an argument for lock duration.

choices.label: Release the lock and allow every miss to load
choices.result: This removes the global lock from user code and can be a sound, useful cache policy. It also allows duplicate loads for the same key, so it fails the one-active-loader requirement as stated. If duplicate pure work is acceptable, this simpler policy may be the right tradeoff; external effects need additional care.

choices.label: Install a per-key loading state and coordinate waiters
choices.result: Publish ready or failed and wake waiters even if a load panics or is abandoned. Run loaders outside the global lock and impose a fixed key order: a loader may request only higher-ranked keys. Reject other nested requests before starting or waiting on a load. This prevents self-waits and cross-key cycles such as A waiting for B while B waits for A.

rooms.remix: Let callers cancel while waiting and permit the initiating loader to disappear. Explain how waiters get a terminal outcome and when they can retry. Test two simultaneous loaders that request each other's keys and identify which request must fail.
